sections.heading: Where the WAH! story begins
sections.body:
WAH! Spices was born in Surat, and Gujarat is where our idea of a good masala comes from. A Gujarati kitchen is a lesson in balance: a little sweetness from jaggery, a little sourness from kokum, lemon or tamarind, and spices used to lift the food rather than bury it.

That balance depends on spices that are fresh and honestly made. Many of the seed spices we use every day — jeera, saunf, dhania, ajwain, methi — grow in Gujarat and its neighbouring states, so the story of our masalas really starts in these fields.
sections.imageAlt: A Gujarati thali with many small bowls
sections.imageCaption: A Gujarati thali: dal, kadhi, shaak, rotli and rice, with something sweet, sour and spicy on every plate.

sections.heading: Unjha and the seed-spice belt
sections.body:
North Gujarat — the districts around Mehsana, Patan and Banaskantha — is one of India's great seed-spice belts. The town of Unjha has one of the country's busiest spice market yards, where farmers bring cumin, fennel, isabgol and other seeds after the harvest.

Cumin is sown after the monsoon, once the heat breaks, and is harvested in late winter. It likes dry, cool weather; a humid spell can bring disease, so every season is a gamble on the sky. After harvest the plants are dried and threshed, and the seeds are cleaned and graded before they reach a spice kitchen.

Gujarat and neighbouring Rajasthan together grow most of India's cumin, which is why jeera turns up in nearly every Gujarati dish — in the tempering, in buttermilk, and roasted and ground into dhana-jiru.
sections.imageCaption: Cumin is a cool-season crop: it needs dry, sunny winters to ripen well.
sections.imageCredit: Photo: Tanvir Anjum Adib · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

sections.heading: Saunf and isabgol
sections.body:
Fennel grows tall and feathery, with umbrella-shaped seed heads. For the best saunf, the heads are cut when the seeds are fully formed but still green, then dried away from harsh sun so they keep their colour and their sweet, anise-like aroma. Gujarat is one of the leading fennel-growing states in India.

After a Gujarati meal you will almost always be offered mukhwas — fennel seeds, sometimes roasted with sesame or coated in sugar — to freshen the mouth and help digestion.

Isabgol, or psyllium, is another winter crop of the region. Its seeds are milled to separate the husk, which is used as a natural fibre. India is the world's main producer of psyllium, and most of it is grown in Gujarat and Rajasthan.
sections.imageCaption: Fennel seed heads are cut and dried in the shade so the seeds stay green and sweet.
sections.imageCredit: Photo: Holly Cheng · CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

sections.heading: Dhana-jiru and the art of the vaghar
sections.body:
If one blend defines Gujarati home cooking, it is dhana-jiru: coriander and cumin seeds, lightly roasted and ground together. It goes into dals, shaak (vegetable dishes), kadhi and farsan, usually alongside turmeric (haldar) and red chilli (marchu).

Most dishes begin or end with a vaghar — a tempering of mustard seeds, cumin, a pinch of asafoetida, dried red chillies and curry leaves sizzled in hot oil or ghee and poured over the food. The order matters: mustard seeds first until they pop, then cumin, then the rest for just a few seconds so nothing burns.

sections.heading: Undhiyu: winter in a pot
sections.body:
Undhiyu takes its name from 'undhu', meaning upside down: traditionally the pot was sealed and buried upside down in a pit of embers, so the vegetables cooked slowly in their own steam.

The Surti version uses winter vegetables — surti papdi beans, purple yam, sweet potato, raw banana and baby brinjals — together with methi muthiya, small fried dumplings of fenugreek leaves and gram flour. Everything is coated in a green masala of fresh coriander, coconut, green garlic, green chilli and ginger, with ajwain, sesame and a balanced blend of dry spices.

It is the dish of Uttarayan, the kite festival in January, when families spend the day on the rooftops and undhiyu with puri and jalebi waits downstairs.
sections.imageCaption: Undhiyu is a winter speciality, eaten especially around Uttarayan (Makar Sankranti).

sections.heading: Chaas, pickles and methia masala
sections.body:
Summer in Gujarat means chaas: thin buttermilk churned with water and seasoned with roasted cumin, black salt, fresh coriander or mint and sometimes a little ginger. It is drunk with lunch almost everywhere.

Summer is also pickle season. Raw mangoes are cut and mixed with methia masala — split fenugreek seeds, split mustard seeds, red chilli, turmeric, asafoetida and salt — then layered with oil and left to mature. Each family has its own proportions, and the jars last the whole year.

sections.heading: Cooking for the desert
sections.body:
In the Thar desert, water is precious and fresh vegetables are scarce for much of the year. Rajasthani cooks answered with ingredients that keep: dried beans and berries, gram flour, millet, ghee, yoghurt and buttermilk — and plenty of spices, which add flavour and help food last.

The royal kitchens of the Rajput courts added their own grandeur: game cooked over fire, rich gravies and elaborate sweets. Today that heritage lives on in the dhabas and homes of Jodhpur, Jaipur, Bikaner and Udaipur.

sections.heading: Cumin and coriander country
sections.body:
Rajasthan is one of India's biggest seed-spice states. Cumin grows across the western districts around Jodhpur, Barmer, Jalore and Nagaur, where the dry winters suit it well. Together with Gujarat, the state grows most of the country's jeera.

In the south-east, the Hadoti region around Kota, Baran and Jhalawar is known for coriander. Ramganj Mandi, near Kota, is one of the largest coriander markets in India. The seeds are dried on the plant, threshed and cleaned; roasting them just before grinding releases their warm, citrusy aroma.
sections.imageCaption: Coriander is grown for its seed in the Hadoti region of south-east Rajasthan.
sections.imageCredit: Photo: Sanjay Acharya · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

sections.heading: Mathania chilli and laal maas
sections.body:
Mathania, a village near Jodhpur, gave its name to a long, deep-red chilli known for colour and aroma as much as for heat. Chillies like these are the soul of laal maas — 'red meat' — the most famous dish of Rajasthani royal cooking.

For laal maas, mutton is cooked slowly with a generous amount of red chilli, garlic, yoghurt, coriander and whole spices in ghee. Some cooks finish it with dhungar: a hot piece of charcoal placed in a small bowl inside the pot, drizzled with ghee and covered for a few minutes so the curry takes on a gentle smoky aroma.
sections.imageCaption: Laal maas gets its colour from plenty of red chillies cooked slowly in ghee.
sections.imageCredit: Photo: Richard Mortel · CC BY 2.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

sections.heading: Kasuri methi from Nagaur
sections.body:
Kasuri methi — dried fenugreek leaves — is named after Kasur, a town now in Pakistan, but in India it is Nagaur in Rajasthan that is famous for it. Nagaur's fenugreek is grown in winter, and the leaves are dried to keep their colour and strong, slightly bitter, maple-like aroma.

Crush a pinch between your palms and add it at the end of cooking: it transforms butter masala, dal, paneer gravies and parathas. A little goes a long way.
sections.imageCaption: Fresh fenugreek leaves are dried to make kasuri methi.

sections.heading: Dal baati churma and ker sangri
sections.body:
Baati are hard dumplings of wheat flour and ghee, traditionally baked in the embers of a fire, then cracked open and soaked in ghee. They are served with panchmel dal, made from five lentils and tempered with cumin, asafoetida and red chilli, and with churma — crushed baati sweetened with jaggery or sugar.

Ker sangri is pure desert cooking: ker, a small wild berry, and sangri, the beans of the khejri tree, are dried after harvest and later cooked with red chilli, cumin, amchur and oil. It keeps for months and tastes of the land.
sections.imageCaption: Dal baati churma — baked baati, five-lentil dal and sweet churma.
sections.imageCredit: Photo: Mahi Tatavarty · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

sections.heading: The granary of India
sections.body:
Punjab means 'land of five waters', after the rivers that cross the region. Its irrigated plains are among the most productive farmland in India: wheat grows through the winter and rice through the monsoon, and in late winter the mustard fields bloom bright yellow.

Punjabi food reflects that abundance. Meals are hearty and generous, built on wheat rotis and parathas, lentils and beans, fresh dairy — lassi, white butter, paneer and ghee — and the greens of the season.
sections.imageCaption: In late winter, mustard fields bloom yellow across the Punjab plains.

sections.heading: Chole: the art of the dark masala
sections.body:
Good Punjabi chole are dark, tangy and deeply spiced. The chickpeas are often boiled with a few tea leaves or dried amla in a muslin bag, which gives them their deep brown colour.

The flavour comes from the masala: roasted coriander and cumin, black cardamom, black pepper, cloves and cinnamon, with dried pomegranate seeds (anardana) and dried mango powder (amchur) for sourness. In the Amritsari and Pindi styles the spices are fried in ghee and poured over the chickpeas, then everything is simmered until thick.

Serve with bhature, kulcha or simply with sliced onions, green chillies and lemon.
sections.imageCaption: Chole bhature, a Punjabi breakfast and street-food favourite.

sections.heading: The tandoor
sections.body:
The tandoor is a clay oven heated with charcoal or wood until its walls are blisteringly hot. Breads are slapped onto the inner wall and bake in a minute or two; meat and paneer on skewers cook in its intense, smoky heat.

Villages once shared a common tandoor where families brought their dough to be baked. After 1947, Punjabi cooks who moved to Delhi brought tandoori cooking to restaurants, and dishes like tandoori chicken became famous across India and the world.

A tandoori marinade combines thick yoghurt, ginger-garlic paste, mild red chilli for colour, roasted cumin and coriander, garam masala, kasuri methi and lemon juice or mustard oil.
sections.imageCaption: Rotis and naan are slapped onto the hot inner wall of the clay tandoor.
sections.imageCredit: Photo: Ravi Dwivedi · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

sections.heading: Dal makhani and rajma
sections.body:
Dal makhani is slow food: whole black urad dal and a little rajma, soaked overnight and simmered for hours until creamy, then finished with butter and cream. The masala is gentle — ginger, garlic, tomato, a little red chilli and garam masala — so the lentils can shine.

Rajma-chawal — red kidney beans in an onion-tomato gravy, served with steamed rice — is the comfort food of countless Punjabi homes, especially for Sunday lunch.

sections.heading: Langar: food for everyone
sections.body:
The Sikh tradition of langar — a free community kitchen open to everyone — goes back to Guru Nanak. Visitors of every faith and background sit together on the floor and are served the same simple vegetarian meal: dal, roti, a vegetable and often kheer.

The langar at the Golden Temple in Amritsar is one of the largest in the world. It is cooked and served by volunteers as sewa (selfless service), and it is a moving reminder that food is, above all, something to share.
sections.imageAlt: Cooking cauldrons in the Golden Temple langar kitchen
sections.imageCaption: The langar kitchen at the Golden Temple, where volunteers cook in giant cauldrons.

sections.heading: Awadh and the art of dum
sections.body:
In the 18th and 19th centuries Lucknow was the capital of the Nawabs of Awadh, and its royal kitchens developed one of India's most refined cuisines. Awadhi cooking is about subtlety: fragrance over fire, and patience over speed.

Its signature technique is dum — food sealed in a pot, often with a rim of dough, and cooked very slowly over gentle heat so the meat, rice and spices steam in their own juices. A popular story links dum cooking to the building of Lucknow's Bara Imambara, when large pots of food were kept sealed and warm to feed the workers day and night.
sections.imageCaption: The Bara Imambara in Lucknow, built under the Nawabs of Awadh.

sections.heading: Kebabs that melt
sections.body:
Lucknow is famous for its kebabs. The galouti kebab is made from very finely minced meat mixed with a paste of spices and tenderising ingredients, shaped into small patties and cooked gently on a griddle until it almost melts on the tongue. Legend says it was created for a Nawab who could no longer chew.

The spicing is warm and aromatic rather than hot: green cardamom, mace, nutmeg, cloves, cinnamon, kebab chini, and sometimes a touch of rose or kewra water. Kakori and seekh kebabs follow the same philosophy.
sections.imageAlt: Galouti kebabs cooking on a tawa
sections.imageCaption: Galouti kebabs are cooked gently on a wide griddle.

sections.heading: Rose, kewra and attar
sections.body:
Kannauj, in central Uttar Pradesh, is often called the perfume capital of India. For centuries its distillers have made attar using the traditional deg-bhapka method, distilling roses, kewra and other flowers in copper stills and capturing the fragrance in oil.

That love of fragrance runs through Awadhi food. A few drops of rose or kewra water perfume a biryani or a dessert, and dried rose petals appear in some garam masala and potli (spice bag) blends used to flavour yakhni, the meat stock behind many Awadhi dishes.
sections.imageCaption: Dried rose petals and rose water perfume Awadhi biryanis and desserts.
sections.imageCredit: Photo: Marc Smith · CC BY-SA 2.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

sections.heading: Mint and mango country
sections.body:
Away from the royal kitchens, Uttar Pradesh is a vast agricultural state on the fertile Gangetic plains. It grows more sugarcane than any other state, plenty of wheat and potatoes, and much of the mint that is distilled into menthol oil — a crop that has made India the world's leading mint-oil producer.

In early summer, the orchards of Malihabad near Lucknow are heavy with Dasheri mangoes. Mint and mango come together in the season's chutneys and coolers, like aam panna.
sections.imageCaption: Mint is grown widely across Uttar Pradesh.

sections.heading: From Banaras to Agra: street flavours
sections.body:
Uttar Pradesh's street food is as famous as its royal cuisine. In Banaras, breakfast is kachori-sabzi — crisp kachoris with a spicy potato curry — followed by jalebi. Lucknow has its basket chaat and tikki; Mathura is known for its peda, and Agra for petha, a translucent sweet made from ash gourd.

What connects them is a confident use of chaat masala, roasted cumin, black salt and tangy amchur — the flavours of North Indian street food.

sections.heading: Where the Deccan meets the Mughals
sections.body:
Hyderabad was founded by the Qutb Shahi dynasty in the late 16th century — the Charminar dates from that time — and later became the seat of the Asaf Jahi Nizams. Their court kitchens brought together Persian and Mughal techniques with local Telugu ingredients: tamarind, red chilli, sesame, peanuts and coconut.

The result is Hyderabadi cuisine: rich and royal like Mughlai food, but with a tangy, spicy Deccan edge.

sections.heading: Kacchi dum biryani
sections.body:
Hyderabad's most famous dish is its kacchi ('raw') dum biryani. Meat is marinated with yoghurt, ginger-garlic, green chillies, fried onions, mint, coriander and spices, then layered raw at the bottom of a heavy pot with partly cooked basmati rice on top.

Saffron milk and ghee are drizzled over, the lid is sealed with dough, and the pot cooks slowly on dum. The meat cooks in its own juices and steams the rice above it with flavour.

The spices are whole and fragrant: shahi jeera, green and black cardamom, cloves, cinnamon, bay leaf and mace, often with kebab chini and a few dried rose petals.
sections.imageCaption: In kacchi dum biryani, raw marinated meat and rice cook together in a sealed pot.

sections.heading: Haleem in Ramzan
sections.body:
During Ramzan, Hyderabad's streets fill with haleem stalls. Wheat, lentils and meat are cooked together for hours in large cauldrons and pounded continuously with wooden mallets until the mixture turns smooth and stretchy.

It is finished with ghee, fried onions, mint, lemon and a sprinkle of garam masala. Hyderabadi haleem carries a Geographical Indication tag, recognising it as a speciality of the city.
sections.imageCaption: Haleem is a Ramzan speciality in Hyderabad.

sections.heading: Salan, khatta and the Telugu touch
sections.body:
Hyderabadi cooks love a sour note. Mirchi ka salan — the classic partner to biryani — is made by simmering green chillies in a gravy of roasted peanuts, sesame seeds and dry coconut, sharpened with tamarind. Baghare baingan uses the same nutty, tangy masala with small brinjals.

The 'baghaar' — a tempering of mustard seeds, cumin, curry leaves and dried red chillies in hot oil — finishes many of these dishes, a reminder of the Telugu kitchen at the heart of Hyderabadi food.

sections.heading: Turmeric and chillies from Telangana's fields
sections.body:
Beyond Hyderabad, Telangana is an important spice-growing state. Nizamabad is well known for turmeric: the rhizomes are dug up in winter, boiled, sun-dried for weeks and polished before they go to market and, finally, to the grinder.

Warangal and Khammam are known for red chillies, including plump, mild varieties grown mainly for their bright colour. Together, turmeric and red chilli give Telangana's food its warm colour and gentle heat.
sections.imageCaption: Fresh turmeric rhizomes are boiled, dried and polished before grinding.
sections.imageCredit: Photo: Emőke Dénes · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

sections.heading: Guntur: a sea of red
sections.body:
Drive through Guntur district in early spring and you will see whole fields turned red: freshly picked chillies spread out on the ground to dry in the sun. Guntur is one of the largest chilli-growing regions in India, and its market yard is among the biggest chilli trading centres in Asia.

Chillies are planted after the monsoon and picked in several rounds through winter and spring as the pods ripen to red. Drying them well is essential — properly dried chillies keep their colour and flavour and store safely until they are ground.
sections.imageAlt: Red chillies drying in Guntur district
sections.imageCaption: Chillies drying in the sun at a village in Guntur district.

sections.heading: Heat and colour: how chillies are graded
sections.body:
Not all chillies are made for the same job. Some varieties are grown for fierce heat, others for deep colour with gentle heat, and many fall somewhere in between. Andhra and Telangana grow some of India's hottest commercial varieties, as well as milder ones used mainly for colour.

Traders judge dried chillies by their pungency, their colour, their skin and their moisture. Stems are removed (for 'stemless' grades), damaged pods are sorted out, and the chillies are then ground into powder or sold whole. A good chilli powder starts with good sorting.

sections.heading: Avakaya and gongura: the pickle tradition
sections.body:
No Andhra meal is complete without pickle. Avakaya, the most famous, is made in early summer from hard, sour raw mangoes, cut with the stone and mixed with mustard powder, red chilli powder, salt and sesame or groundnut oil. Families make it in large batches and it lasts the whole year.

Gongura — the leaves of the roselle plant — has a sharp, sour taste and is loved across Andhra and Telangana as pickle and as pachadi (chutney), often with plenty of red chilli and garlic.
sections.imageCaption: Every Andhra home has its own pickle recipes and jars.

sections.heading: Karam podi and the tiffin plate
sections.body:
Karam podi, sometimes called 'gunpowder', is a coarse dry powder of roasted urad and chana dal, dried red chillies, garlic, cumin and curry leaves. Mixed with a spoon of ghee or sesame oil, it turns a plate of idli, dosa or pesarattu into something special.

Andhra kitchens make many podis — with curry leaves, with flaxseed, with dals — and they are eaten with hot rice and ghee too.
sections.imageCaption: Podi mixed with ghee or sesame oil is the classic partner for idli and dosa.
sections.imageCredit: Photo: Karthik Sridhar · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

sections.heading: Tamarind and pulihora
sections.body:
Tamarind is the sour backbone of Andhra food, in rasam, pulusu (tangy stews) and, most famously, pulihora. To make it, cooked rice is mixed with thick tamarind paste and a tempering of mustard seeds, chana and urad dal, peanuts, dried red chillies, curry leaves, turmeric and asafoetida.

Pulihora is prepared for festivals and offered as prasadam in temples. It keeps well, which made it a traditional food for journeys too.
sections.imageCaption: Pulihora — tamarind rice with peanuts, curry leaves and a mustard-seed tempering.

sections.heading: Byadgi: colour without the fire
sections.body:
Byadgi, a town in Haveri district in north Karnataka, gives its name to one of India's best-known chillies and is home to a large chilli market. Byadgi chilli has a Geographical Indication tag.

The pods are long, thin and deeply wrinkled, with a dark red colour and relatively mild heat. That makes them perfect when you want a dish to look rich and red without making it too hot — in South Indian sambars, chutneys and curries. Their natural red pigment is also extracted as an oleoresin used to colour foods.
sections.imageCaption: Byadgi chillies are known for their wrinkled skin and deep red colour.
sections.imageCredit: Photo: GI tagged products · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

sections.heading: Coorg: spices in the coffee shade
sections.body:
Kodagu, better known as Coorg, sits high in the Western Ghats. Its coffee estates are planted under tall shade trees, and black pepper vines are trained to climb those trees — so one estate produces two crops, and the forest canopy is kept alive.

Pepper is harvested in winter when the berry spikes start to turn red. The berries are separated and dried in the sun until they shrivel and turn black. In the cooler, shadier valleys, green cardamom grows too; Coorg green cardamom has its own Geographical Indication tag.
sections.imageAlt: A coffee and pepper estate in Coorg
sections.imageCaption: In Coorg, coffee grows under tall shade trees, and pepper vines climb those trees.

sections.heading: Bisi bele bath and the Mysore kitchen
sections.body:
Bisi bele bath means 'hot lentil rice' in Kannada, and it is the pride of the Mysuru region. Rice and toor dal are cooked with vegetables and tamarind, then simmered with a special spice powder of Byadgi chillies, coriander seeds, chana and urad dal, fenugreek, cinnamon, cloves and dry coconut.

Finished with a ghee tempering of mustard seeds, curry leaves and cashews, it is served piping hot. Mysuru also gave the world Mysore pak — a rich sweet of gram flour, sugar and ghee — and the Mysore masala dosa with its spicy red chutney.
sections.imageCaption: Bisi bele bath is served hot with ghee and crunchy boondi or papad.
sections.imageCredit: Photo: Food and Remedy, LLC · CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

sections.heading: The coast: kokum, coconut and ghee roast
sections.body:
Along the coast, from Mangaluru to Karwar, cooking changes again. Coconut, fresh fish and kokum — the sour, purple fruit of a Western Ghats tree, dried for use in curries and drinks — take centre stage.

Mangalorean ghee roast is made by roasting Byadgi chillies with coriander, cumin, pepper, fenugreek and garlic, grinding them with tamarind and cooking the paste slowly in plenty of ghee with chicken or prawns. Nearby, the temple town of Udupi is famous for its vegetarian cooking — saaru, huli and dosas — Udupi is often credited as the birthplace of the masala dosa.
sections.imageAlt: A Mangalorean fish meal on a banana leaf
sections.imageCaption: A coastal Karnataka meal: fish curry, rice and fried fish on a banana leaf.

sections.heading: The coast the world sailed to
sections.body:
Long before Europe had heard of chillies, the Malabar coast of Kerala was the source of the world's black pepper. Traders from Rome, Arabia, China and beyond came for it; the ancient port of Muziris, near today's Kodungallur, was famous across the ancient world.

In 1498 the Portuguese navigator Vasco da Gama landed near Kozhikode (Calicut), opening a sea route from Europe to India that changed world history — largely because of spices. In Kochi's old quarter, spice warehouses still line the streets, and the smell of pepper, ginger and cardamom hangs in the air.
sections.imageAlt: A Chinese fishing net at Kochi
sections.imageCaption: Chinese fishing nets at Kochi, a port that has traded in spices for centuries.
sections.imageCredit: Photo: Hans A. Rosbach · CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

sections.heading: Malabar pepper: black gold
sections.body:
Black pepper grows on a climbing vine native to the Western Ghats. In Kerala it is often grown in homestead gardens, trained up coconut palms, jackfruit trees and other supports.

The berries grow on long spikes and are picked in winter, when a few on each spike begin to turn red. They are separated from the spikes and dried in the sun for several days, turning black and wrinkled as they dry. White pepper is made from the same berries by soaking them and removing the outer skin.

Malabar pepper has a Geographical Indication tag. Freshly ground, it has a bright, piney heat that pre-ground pepper quickly loses.
sections.imageCaption: Pepper berries ripen on long spikes; dried in the sun, they turn black and wrinkled.

sections.heading: The Cardamom Hills
sections.body:
High in the Western Ghats, in Idukki district, are the Cardamom Hills. Green cardamom is a shade-loving plant related to ginger; its capsules grow on shoots near the ground and ripen a few at a time, so they are picked by hand in rounds through the season.

The freshly picked capsules are cured in drying sheds with gentle heat, which helps them keep their green colour and their sweet, cooling aroma. Cardamom is one of the world's most valuable spices, and it flavours everything from chai and biryani to payasam.
sections.imageCaption: Cardamom grows in the cool, shaded hills of the Western Ghats.

sections.heading: Nutmeg, mace, cloves and ginger
sections.body:
The nutmeg tree gives two spices. When its fruit splits open, it reveals a dark seed — the nutmeg — wrapped in a lacy red covering called mace (javitri). The two are separated and dried; the mace fades to orange-gold, and the nutmeg is dried in its shell.

Cloves are the dried flower buds of an evergreen tree, picked before they open. Kerala's ginger has been traded as dry ginger for centuries: the rhizomes are peeled, washed and sun-dried, giving the warm, sharp spice called saunth.
sections.imageCaption: Inside the nutmeg fruit, the seed is wrapped in bright red mace.

sections.heading: The Kerala table
sections.body:
Kerala cooking is built on coconut — oil, milk and grated flesh — along with curry leaves, mustard seeds, shallots and the spices of the hills. Fish curries are soured with kudampuli (Malabar tamarind) and coloured with red chilli; meat is often slow-roasted with a heap of crushed black pepper.

The sadya, served at Onam and weddings, is a vegetarian feast on a banana leaf: rice with sambar, avial, olan, thoran, pickles and two or three kinds of payasam. In the north, Malabar is famous for its biryani, made with short-grain kaima rice and fragrant whole spices.
sections.imageAlt: A Kerala sadya on a banana leaf
sections.imageCaption: A sadya is served on a banana leaf with many dishes, eaten in a set order.

sections.heading: Erode: the turmeric city
sections.body:
Erode, in western Tamil Nadu, is one of India's most important turmeric centres, and Erode turmeric has a Geographical Indication tag. Turmeric is planted from pieces of rhizome and takes most of a year to mature.

After harvest, the rhizomes are boiled or steamed, which sets their colour and aroma, then dried in the sun for a couple of weeks until they are hard. Finally they are polished to remove the rough outer skin. The deep yellow colour comes from curcumin, and good turmeric should smell earthy and warm, never musty.
sections.imageCaption: Turmeric grows from underground rhizomes and is harvested after about nine months.
sections.imageCredit: Photo: Thamizhpparithi Maari · CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

sections.heading: Sambar and rasam podi
sections.body:
Every Tamil household has its own sambar podi and rasam podi, often made in batches and stored in tins. A typical sambar podi roasts coriander seeds, dried red chillies, chana and toor dal, fenugreek, cumin, black pepper and curry leaves, then grinds them with turmeric and asafoetida.

Sambar combines toor dal, vegetables, tamarind and this podi; rasam is lighter — a thin, peppery broth of tamarind, tomato, pepper and cumin that is drunk as much as eaten. Together with rice, they are the backbone of the Tamil meal.
sections.imageCaption: Sambar: lentils, vegetables and tamarind with a freshly made podi.

sections.heading: Chettinad: the spice merchants' kitchen
sections.body:
The Chettinad region around Karaikudi is home to the Nattukottai Chettiars, a merchant community whose trade once stretched across Burma, Sri Lanka and South-East Asia. Their grand mansions and their cooking are famous.

Chettinad food is known for bold, freshly ground masalas. Alongside black pepper, red chilli, fennel and star anise, cooks use unusual spices such as kalpasi (dagad phool, a lichen with a deep, earthy aroma) and marathi mokku (dried flower buds). Chettinad pepper chicken shows the style perfectly: fiery, fragrant and rich.
sections.imageCaption: The Chettiars' trading history shaped one of India's most aromatic cuisines.
sections.imageCredit: Photo: Rainer Halama · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

sections.heading: Tamarind, curry leaves and the thalippu
sections.body:
The thalippu (tempering) is where Tamil flavour begins or ends: mustard seeds popped in hot oil, then urad dal for crunch, dried red chilli, a pinch of asafoetida and a handful of fresh curry leaves that crackle and release their aroma.

Tamarind (puli) adds the sourness that runs through Tamil food — in sambar, rasam, kuzhambu and puliyodarai. Many homes still keep a curry-leaf tree by the kitchen door.
sections.imageCaption: Fresh curry leaves go into almost every Tamil tempering.
sections.imageCredit: Photo: Flocci Nivis · CC BY 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

sections.heading: Temple kitchens and festival food
sections.body:
Tamil Nadu's great temples have kitchens that have cooked offerings (prasadam) for centuries. Puliyodarai, sakkarai pongal (sweet rice with jaggery, ghee and cardamom) and ven pongal (savoury rice and moong dal with pepper, cumin and ghee) are temple classics.

At Pongal, the January harvest festival, families cook the new season's rice with milk and jaggery in a pot until it boils over — a sign of abundance for the year ahead.

sections.heading: Mumbai on a tawa
sections.body:
Mumbai's most famous street dish is pav bhaji. Popular history traces it to the city's textile mills, where workers needed a quick, filling and cheap meal late in the day. Vendors mashed whatever vegetables were left — potatoes, peas, tomatoes, capsicum, cauliflower — with butter and a special spice blend on a huge flat tawa, and served it with soft bread rolls (pav) toasted in more butter.

Pav bhaji masala is built on coriander, cumin, fennel, red chilli, dried mango, black salt and warm spices like cinnamon, cloves and black cardamom. A squeeze of lemon and chopped onion finish it.
sections.imageCaption: Pav bhaji is cooked on a huge flat tawa with plenty of butter.
sections.imageCredit: Photo: Ashwin Kumar · CC BY-SA 2.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

sections.heading: The city's street-food heroes
sections.body:
Vada pav — a spiced potato fritter in a pav with dry garlic chutney and fried green chillies — is often called Mumbai's burger. Then there is bhel puri on the beach, pani puri with tangy mint water, and the Bombay sandwich: buttered bread layered with green chutney, potato, cucumber, tomato and onion, dusted with sandwich masala.

What ties them together is a set of bold blends — chaat masala, pani puri masala, sandwich masala — designed to hit sour, salty, spicy and fresh all at once.
sections.imageAlt: Vada pav with a fried green chilli
sections.imageCaption: Vada pav, Mumbai's favourite street snack.
sections.imageCredit: Photo: Rutvi Mistry · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

sections.heading: Goda masala: the sweet-smoky blend
sections.body:
Goda masala is the signature blend of Maharashtrian homes. Coriander seeds, sesame seeds and dry coconut are roasted until dark, along with cinnamon, cloves, cardamom, bay leaf, dagad phool and dried red chillies, then ground together. The result is dark, nutty and slightly sweet rather than hot.

A spoonful goes into amti (a tangy dal with kokum or tamarind and jaggery), masale bhaat (spiced rice with vegetables) and vegetable dishes like bharli vangi — stuffed brinjals.

sections.heading: Kolhapur's fire
sections.body:
Kolhapur, in southern Maharashtra, is famous for its fiery food. Its mutton is served with two broths: tambda rassa, red with chillies and spice, and pandhra rassa, a soothing white broth made with coconut milk.

Misal pav, eaten across the state, is a curry of sprouted moth beans topped with a spicy, oily gravy called kat or tarri, crunchy farsan, onion and coriander, served with pav. Kolhapuri masala and kanda-lasun masala — a blend of onion, garlic, red chilli and spices — give these dishes their kick.
sections.imageCaption: Misal: a spicy sprouted-bean curry topped with farsan, onion and coriander.

sections.heading: Konkan: kokum and coconut
sections.body:
Along the Konkan coast, in Ratnagiri and Sindhudurg, the kokum tree grows in the hills near the sea. Its purple fruit is cut and the rind is sun-dried — often soaked in its own juice and salt — to make amsul, which gives a gentle, fruity sourness to fish curries and dals.

Sol kadhi, a pink drink of kokum and coconut milk with garlic and green chilli, is served after a Malvani meal to cool the palate. The same coast is home to the Alphonso mango, and further inland Sangli is one of India's largest turmeric markets.
sections.imageCaption: Sol kadhi — kokum and coconut milk — served after a Konkan meal.

sections.heading: Where India's tea began
sections.body:
The tea plant grows wild in the hills of Upper Assam, and local communities such as the Singpho were drinking it long before tea gardens existed. In the 1820s the plant was recorded by British visitors, and by the 1830s and 1840s the first commercial gardens were being planted in the Brahmaputra valley.

Today the valley is covered in neat green tea gardens. Pluckers move along the rows picking 'two leaves and a bud' from the top of each bush; the leaves are withered, rolled or cut, oxidised and dried in the factory. Assam tea is known for its strong, malty, full-bodied cup.
sections.imageCaption: Pluckers pick 'two leaves and a bud' from the top of each tea bush.

sections.heading: Masala chai, the Indian way
sections.body:
Strong Assam tea is the base of India's favourite drink, masala chai. Tea leaves are boiled with water, milk and sugar along with spices: crushed green cardamom and ginger above all, often with cloves, cinnamon and black pepper, and sometimes tulsi or fennel.

Every family and every chai stall has its own balance. In winter, a little dry ginger (saunth) and extra pepper make it especially warming.
sections.imageCaption: Masala chai: strong tea, milk, sugar and warming spices.

sections.heading: Bhut jolokia
sections.body:
Assam and its neighbours in the North-East grow the bhut jolokia, also called the ghost pepper or king chilli. In the 2000s it was recognised as the world's hottest chilli, and although hotter hybrids have since been bred, it remains one of the most powerful chillies anywhere.

In Assamese and North-Eastern kitchens it is used with great care — a sliver in a chutney or pickle, or a whole chilli briefly dipped into a curry and removed. Its heat comes with a fruity, smoky flavour.
sections.imageCaption: Bhut jolokia is grown in Assam and its neighbouring north-eastern states.
sections.imageCredit: Photo: Chiring chandan · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

sections.heading: Tenga, khar and pitika
sections.body:
Assamese cooking is light and clean, using mustard oil, fresh herbs and only a few spices so that the ingredients can shine. Masor tenga is a sour fish curry, made tangy with tomatoes, lemon or elephant apple. Khar, made with an alkaline extract from dried banana peel, is traditionally eaten at the start of a meal.

Pitika are simple mashes — of potato, aubergine or fish — mixed with raw mustard oil, onion and green chilli. When spices are used, panch phoron (fenugreek, nigella, cumin, mustard and fennel) and ginger are favourites.
sections.imageCaption: Assamese food uses few spices and lets fresh ingredients lead.
sections.imageCredit: Photo: Nilotpal Hazarika · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)

regions.name: Jammu & Kashmir
regions.cardText: The purple crocus fields of Pampore, ruby-red Kashmiri chillies and the grand Wazwan feast — Kashmir's flavours are fragrant, rich and unhurried.

sections.heading: The saffron of Pampore
sections.body:
Every autumn, the plateaus (karewas) around Pampore, south of Srinagar, turn purple with the flowers of the saffron crocus. They bloom for only a few weeks, usually from late October into November.

The flowers are picked by hand early in the morning. Each one holds just three crimson stigmas, which are pulled out by hand and dried carefully. It takes a huge number of flowers to make a small amount of saffron, which is why it is one of the most precious spices in the world. Kashmir saffron has a Geographical Indication tag.

Good saffron has long, deep-red threads, a honeyed, hay-like aroma and releases a golden colour slowly when soaked in warm milk or water.
sections.imageCaption: Each crocus flower holds three crimson stigmas — the saffron.

sections.heading: Kashmiri chilli: colour over fire
sections.body:
Kashmiri chilli is famous for what it does not do: it is not very hot. What it gives instead is a deep, glowing red colour and a mild, fruity flavour. In autumn, chillies are strung into garlands and hung to dry in the sun.

This is the chilli that gives rogan josh its colour. Much of the 'Kashmiri chilli' sold across India today comes from similar mild, red varieties grown in other states — prized for the same reason: rich colour with gentle heat.
sections.imageCaption: Mild, deep-red chillies of the Kashmiri type are prized for colour rather than heat.

sections.heading: Wazwan: the royal feast
sections.body:
Wazwan is Kashmir's grand ceremonial feast, prepared for weddings and celebrations by master cooks called waza. It can run to many courses, served on a large shared copper platter called a trami, usually for four guests.

The dishes include rista (pounded-meat balls in a red gravy), rogan josh, yakhni (meat in a fennel-scented yoghurt gravy) and finally gushtaba, soft meatballs in yoghurt. The meat for rista and gushtaba is pounded by hand with wooden mallets until it is completely smooth.
sections.imageCaption: Rogan josh, one of the signature dishes of the Wazwan feast.

sections.heading: Fennel, dry ginger and ver
sections.body:
Kashmiri spicing is distinctive. Many Kashmiri Pandit dishes use no onion or garlic, relying instead on ground fennel (saunf), dry ginger (saunth), asafoetida, Kashmiri chilli and yoghurt. The result is fragrant and warming.

Kashmiri Muslim cooking often uses ver — a traditional spice cake. Ground spices such as red chilli, fennel, ginger, cardamom and cloves are mixed with mustard oil and sometimes shallots, shaped into rings or discs and dried. Pieces are broken off and added to curries.

sections.heading: Kahwa and the cold valley
sections.body:
On cold Kashmiri mornings, kahwa is everywhere. Green tea leaves are brewed with saffron threads, crushed green cardamom and cinnamon, then poured into small cups over slivered almonds, often sweetened with sugar or honey. Traditionally it is made in a brass samovar that keeps it hot for hours.

The valley's orchards add walnuts, almonds and apples to the Kashmiri pantry, and the high hills give shahi jeera (black cumin), a finer, darker cousin of everyday cumin.
sections.imageCaption: Kahwa is traditionally brewed in a samovar.
sections.imageCredit: Photo: Sayantan Sarkar · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
